Judyth Vary Baker says she knew Lee Harvey Oswald in New Orleans in 1963 and worked beside him in a covert cancer research project. On Danny Jones's podcast, the JFK witness tells her story. She argues that the top secret CIA files on the assassination will never be released. In her account, they would expose the plot she describes.

Baker's account has been disputed since she first published it, and historians of the assassination mostly reject her claims. Jones hears her out at the length her supporters have always wanted. The episode preserves her testimony as she gives it, unendorsed. For students of the Kennedy case, the value is hearing a controversial witness's complete presentation in her own voice. She gives it late in her life. It beats the summaries written by her critics or her believers.

Physicist Ronald Mallett joins Danny Jones to lay out exactly how he would build a time machine. Mallett is a professor who has spent his life on the physics of time loops. His drive is deep: he lost his father as a boy.

Mallett explains his plan to bend light into a loop that could send word back in time. He tells what the math grants and what the lab still lacks. Jones asks what he would say to his young self if the machine worked. Listeners get a tender, sharp tour of real time science. The library holds the talk as an archive record.

Economist Jeffrey Sachs returns to Tucker Carlson with a scorecard of the three most important things Trump has done so far. Sachs, a Columbia professor, has advised governments worldwide for decades. Here he also weighs America's global dominance and the crossroads it faces.

Sachs picks the moves he believes will define Trump's place in history, for good or ill. He argues the country's power is fading faster than its leaders admit. Carlson asks what choices could still change the path. Serious and political viewers get a veteran's judgment on a presidency and an empire.
